stem: A client who uses a continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion pump is reviewing infusion-site care with the nurse. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.A: I will inspect the infusion site for skin problems, rotate sites, and change the infusion set according to my pump manufacturer’s instructions.
options.B: I should keep using the same infusion site until insulin delivery stops because routine site rotation is unnecessary.
options.C: A pump infusion site does not need skin assessment because infection occurs only with insulin injections, not infusion sets.
options.D: I should use a fixed universal change interval even if the instructions for my specific infusion set recommend something different.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care identify appropriate care and rotation of insulin infusion sites as part of safe insulin administration and note pump-site infection and other skin complications as recognized problems. FDA guidance instructs pump users to follow pump-specific directions for when to change infusion sets and rotate infusion sites. B and C ignore known infusion-site complications. D is incorrect because change timing is device- and infusion-set-specific rather than a single universal interval for every product.
educational_objective: Teach insulin-pump users to inspect and rotate infusion sites and to change infusion sets according to the specific device manufacturer’s instructions rather than relying on a universal change interval.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association; U.S. Food and Drug Administration
source_document_title: Pharmacologic Approaches to Glycemic Treatment: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; Insulin Pumps: Tips for Using Your Insulin Pump at Home
source_version_date: ADA Standards of Care 2026; current FDA pump guidance accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: ADA 2026 Section 9, ‘Insulin Administration Technique’ — proper technique includes infusion-site rotation and care to avoid infection/other complications; Section 7 notes pump-site infection as a recognized complication. FDA ‘Using your insulin pump’ — follow pump-specific instructions for when to change infusion sets and rotate infusion sites
source_claim_supported: Safe insulin-pump use includes appropriate infusion-site care and rotation, recognition of site complications, and following manufacturer-specific instructions for infusion-set changes rather than a universal replacement interval.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies; safely manage medication-delivery devices and provide client education on parenteral therapy
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin-pump infusion-site care
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item and removed the unsourced ‘typically every 2–3 days’ universal timing claim. Current FDA guidance makes infusion-set change timing pump-specific, while ADA 2026 directly supports site rotation and monitoring for skin/infection complications. The item was reclassified from infection control to Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies because it centers on safe insulin-delivery-device management.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against ADA Standards of Care 2026 and current FDA insulin-pump guidance. Both support site care/rotation; FDA explicitly directs users to pump-specific change instructions.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A contains only supported site-inspection/rotation and manufacturer-specific change guidance. No unsupported fixed interval, antiseptic product, or infection-treatment protocol is introduced.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; routine site rotation and scheduled infusion-set changes are part of safe pump use.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; pump-site infection and skin complications are recognized.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; timing depends on the specific pump/infusion-set instructions.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A integrates site surveillance, rotation, and product-specific change instructions without overgeneralization.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address infusion-site management and change timing.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies is appropriate because the construct is safe management of an insulin-delivery system.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked infection-versus-irritation wording, universal 2–3-day interval risk, manufacturer-specific instructions, pump-site complications, category mapping, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
